source_text: Quamquam mihi, ut de statu explicando immorer parvulorum, consequentia rationis indicit, quae res sua lege coniunctas dividi non sinit. Ceterum facilior esset iactura nascentium, si non eis compericlitaretur ipsa maiestas. Excusa igitur Deum, et accusa parvulum; iustum doceatur ille quod facit, qui sine iustitia Deus esse non potest; et quaevis suscipiat persona supplicium. Ceterum nunc extra sacrilegium res, quas putas esse consertas, mutuo sibi vehementer repugnant. Dicis enim, quoniam unis mysteriis, idololatrae ac parricidae, imbuuntur et parvuli, omnes scelestos posse convinci; et addis rem multo absurdiorem, a Sacramenti huius, de quo agimus, auctore aliena peccata innocentibus imputari. Hoc est quod pugnare dixi, quia non capit rerum natura ut uno tempore et adeo sit misericors Deus, ut propria unicuique confitenti peccata condonet; et adeo crudelis, ut innocenti impingat aliena. Horum prorsus cum alterum dederis, alterum sustulisti; si donat veniam reis, non calumniatur innoxiis; si calumniatur innocuis, numquam parcit obnoxiis.
pass_a_gloss: Although to me, that I linger over unfolding the status of little ones, the consequence of reason enjoins, which by its own law does not allow things joined to be divided. For the rest, the loss of those being born would be easier, if the majesty itself were not endangered together with them. Excuse therefore God, and accuse the little one; let him be taught just, what he does, who without justice cannot be God; and let any person you please take up punishment. For the rest now, apart from sacrilege, the things which you think are sewn together mutually fight one another vehemently. For you say that, because by one mysteries idolaters and parricides are imbued and little ones, all can be convicted wicked; and you add a thing much more absurd, that by the author of this Sacrament about which we treat alien sins are imputed to the innocents. This is what I said fights, because the nature of things does not take it that at one time God is both so merciful that he condones to each confessing his own sins; and so cruel that he dashes another's upon the innocent. Of these outright, when you have given the one, you have taken away the other; if he gives pardon to the guilty, he does not slander the harmless; if he slanders the innocents, he never spares the liable.

pass_b_english: The sequence of reasoning obliges me to linger over explaining the condition of infants, because it does not allow matters joined by its own law to be divided. Otherwise the loss of newborn children would be easier to bear if divine majesty itself were not endangered along with them. Clear God, then, and accuse the infant. Show that what he does is just, since he cannot be God without justice, and let any person you please undergo punishment. As things stand, however, quite apart from their sacrilege, the claims you think fit together fiercely contradict one another. You say that because idolaters, murderers of their own kin, and infants are initiated through the same mysteries, all can be proved wicked. Then you add something far more absurd: that the author of this sacrament we are discussing imputes other people's sins to the innocent. This is the contradiction I named. The nature of things does not permit God at one and the same time to be so merciful that he forgives each person who confesses that person's own sins, and so cruel that he fastens someone else's sins upon an innocent person. Grant either one and you have removed the other. If he gives pardon to the guilty, he does not falsely accuse the innocent. If he falsely accuses the innocent, he never spares the guilty.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
